article_title: What differentiates educational literature? A multimodal fusion approach of transformers and computational linguistics
citation: Jordan J. Bird. (2024). What Differentiates Educational Literature? A Multimodal Fusion Approach of Transformers and Computational Linguistics. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.17593
title: Publicly released UK Key Stage readability dataset of 20,000 balanced text chunks
description: A dataset built from 384 Project Gutenberg books cross-referenced with Lexile scores, segmented into chunks of up to 512 tokens and balanced to 5,000 rows per Key Stage. The article states it "resulted in a full dataset size of 20,000 data objects, with 5,000 belonging to each Key Stage 2, 3, 4, and 5", split 80/20 for training and validation, and released publicly under the MIT license on Kaggle for interdisciplinary reuse.
requirements: Books require an available Lexile score to be retained; Key Stage 1 texts were unavailable and excluded
constraints: The study undersampled the full corpus due to computational resource limits, as the authors state
target_learners: UK Key Stage 2–5 secondary and post-16 English students
target_learning_goals: Matching English literature texts to appropriate educational stages and reading difficulty
examples: Lowest Lexile score in the dataset was 420 (The Monkey's Paw); highest was 1840 (Discourse on the Method)
key_sources: Jordan J. Bird. (2024). What Differentiates Educational Literature? A Multimodal Fusion Approach of Transformers and Computational Linguistics. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.17593

article_title: Students as Radical Agents of Change
citation: Fielding, M. (2001). Students as Radical Agents of Change. Journal of Educational Change, 2, 123–141. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1017949213447
title: UK high school Students as Researchers partnership running since 1996
description: A long-running joint project in a UK high school in which students act as researchers, developed since 1996 and described as still current at the time of writing. The abstract states the paper describes "the still current joint work in a UK high school that has developed since 1996" and gives practical examples of the Students as Researchers approach in that setting.
requirements: Sustained researcher–school partnership over multiple years
examples: Practical examples from the school's project are given in the paper
key_sources: Fielding, M. (2001). Students as Radical Agents of Change. Journal of Educational Change, 2, 123–141. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1017949213447

article_title: Performance of GPT-4o and o1-Pro on United Kingdom Medical Licensing Assessment-style items: a comparative study.
citation: Vakili B, Ahmad A, Zolfaghari M. (2025). Performance of GPT-4o and o1-Pro on United Kingdom Medical Licensing Assessment-style items: a comparative study. Journal of Educational Evaluation for Health Professions. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2025.22.30
title: Curated UKMLA-style item dataset (374 text-based and 20 image-based items from Geeky Medics)
description: The article curates a licensed dataset of UKMLA-style single-best-answer items used to benchmark two LLMs. Of "394 UKMLA-style SBA items" screened, 374 text-only items were included (Dataset 1) and "Twenty image-based items were analyzed separately (Dataset 2)", covering clinical photographs, radiological imaging, electrocardiography, and histopathology slides. Items required a single stem, 5 options, and 1 best answer.
requirements: Items screened by two resident doctors for clear SBA format and relevance to the UKMLA syllabus, with discrepancies resolved by consensus
constraints: Items came from a licensed third-party item bank (Geeky Medics), which may not fully capture the breadth, standard-setting, or item formats of the official exam
target_learners: UK medical students preparing for the UKMLA
target_learning_goals: Applied clinical knowledge across medical specialties assessed by single-best-answer items
examples: Each item was entered verbatim into each model with a standardized prompt requesting only the letter of the chosen option, in a new chat window with default parameters
key_sources: Vakili B, Ahmad A, Zolfaghari M. (2025). Performance of GPT-4o and o1-Pro on United Kingdom Medical Licensing Assessment-style items: a comparative study. Journal of Educational Evaluation for Health Professions. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2025.22.30

article_title: Big data analysis: examination of the relationship between candidates' sociodemographic characteristics and performance in the UK's Membership of the Royal College of Physicians Part 1 examination.
citation: Johnston Peter W., Vieira Rute, Cameron Isobel M., Kumwenda Ben, Walker Kim A., Cleland Jennifer A. (2025). Big data analysis: examination of the relationship between candidates' sociodemographic characteristics and performance in the UK's Membership of the Royal College of Physicians Part 1 examination. Advances in Health Sciences Education 30(1), 53-68. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-024-10406-3
title: UK Medical Education Database (UKMED) linked dataset enabling granular differential-attainment analysis
description: UKMED is a database "which holds educational outcomes for all medical students and postgraduate trainees in approved UK medical schools and training programmes by crosslinking data from several sources, including the Higher Education Statistics Authority (HESA) Limited and the General Medical Council (GMC)". In this study it supplied anonymised, linked sociodemographic, programme, EPM, SJT and MRCP Part 1 records for 6040 graduates, analysed within a secure Data Safe Haven. Researchers can apply for access to the same data via UKMED.
requirements: Data must be stored, handled and analysed within a safe haven in accordance with security, governance and confidentiality standards, as the article describes.
constraints: The article notes big data studies are inevitably limited by the data that are available, including incomplete EPM and SJT recording for earlier cohorts.
target_learners: UK medical students and postgraduate medical trainees
target_learning_goals: Understanding group-level patterns of performance and differential attainment across the medical education pathway
examples: The study extracted records for doctors with a UK primary medical qualification in 2012-2014 who sat MRCP Part 1 before October 2019.
key_sources: Johnston Peter W., Vieira Rute, Cameron Isobel M., Kumwenda Ben, Walker Kim A., Cleland Jennifer A. (2025). Big data analysis: examination of the relationship between candidates' sociodemographic characteristics and performance in the UK's Membership of the Royal College of Physicians Part 1 examination. Advances in Health Sciences Education 30(1), 53-68. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-024-10406-3

article_title: Recommendations from a Working Group on Obesity Care Competencies for Healthcare Education in the UK: A Report by the Steering Committee.
citation: Capehorn Matthew S., Hinchliffe Nigel, Cook Deborah, Hill Andrew, O’Kane Mary, Tahrani Abd A., Vincent Ann, Williams Simon, Feenie John. (2022). Recommendations from a Working Group on Obesity Care Competencies for Healthcare Education in the UK: A Report by the Steering Committee. Advances in Therapy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12325-022-02108-2
title: UK obesity care competency framework organised into five focal areas for specialist obesity care
description: The UK Obesity Care Competencies Working Group devised a framework of obesity care competencies for healthcare professionals involved in specialist obesity care (tiers 2–4 in the UK), adapted from the US OMEC competencies. As the article states, the group "developed a set of 29 competencies, divided into five focal areas, namely obesity knowledge, patient care and procedural skills, practice-based learning and improvement, professionalism and interpersonal communication skills, and systems-based practice". The framework is intended to be adaptable to nurses and allied health professionals as well as physicians, reflecting the UK multidisciplinary team approach.
requirements: HCPs using the framework work in or train for specialist obesity care services (tiers 2–4 in the UK)
constraints: The working group recommends targeting the competencies at medical staff training as specialists; tier 1 prevention competencies are covered separately by Health Education England's Healthier Weight Framework

The paper states a limitation: the lack of inclusion of an external review process by education and professional training boards, and the lack of assessment tools for how the competencies may be assessed
target_learners: Healthcare professionals training as specialists in obesity care, including physicians, nurses and allied health professionals
target_learning_goals: Obesity knowledge, patient care and procedural skills, practice-based learning and improvement, professionalism and interpersonal communication, and systems-based practice in obesity care
examples: The working group met in September 2020, discussed the 32 US OMEC competencies, and refined the UK set over two iterations before agreeing the final 29 competencies
key_sources: Capehorn Matthew S., Hinchliffe Nigel, Cook Deborah, Hill Andrew, O’Kane Mary, Tahrani Abd A., Vincent Ann, Williams Simon, Feenie John. (2022). Recommendations from a Working Group on Obesity Care Competencies for Healthcare Education in the UK: A Report by the Steering Committee. Advances in Therapy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12325-022-02108-2

article_title: How to Introduce Scopemanship Into Your Training Program.
citation: Bollipo Steven, Bilal Mohammad, Siau Keith, Charabaty Aline. (2020). How to Introduce Scopemanship Into Your Training Program. Gastroenterology. https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2020.08.013
title: UK Direct Observation of Procedural Skills assessments covering nontechnical qualities
description: The United Kingdom direct observation of procedural skills assessments are workplace-based assessment tools that, according to the article, "assess qualities of leadership, situational awareness, judgement and decision making, and communication in both formative and summative contexts." The article recommends using such formative assessment tools to gauge performance and set future objectives, and suggests incorporating "objective feedback from nursing staff and patients" into the evaluation to reflect and improve practice.
requirements: Assessment and feedback are essential to maximize benefit from hands-on training
target_learners: Endoscopy trainees in the United Kingdom
target_learning_goals: Leadership, situational awareness, judgement and decision making, and communication
examples: The article proposes assessing scopemanship competencies during endoscopy to provide feedback and set objectives for personal development
key_sources: Bollipo Steven, Bilal Mohammad, Siau Keith, Charabaty Aline. (2020). How to Introduce Scopemanship Into Your Training Program. Gastroenterology. https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2020.08.013

article_title: Changing Autonomy in Operative Experience Through UK General Surgery Training: A National Cohort Study.
citation: Elsey EJ, Griffiths G, West J, Humes DJ. (2018). Changing Autonomy in Operative Experience Through UK General Surgery Training: A National Cohort Study. Annals of Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1097/SLA.0000000000003032
title: Linked national surgical training databases (ISCP, eLogbook, JCST SIMS, JCIE) as a data source for cohort competency analysis
description: This is the set of mandatory UK repositories the study linked by GMC number: the ISCP database (training dates, PBA records), the JCST SIMS database (out-of-programme periods), the Joint Committee on Intercollegiate Examinations database (special interest at examination), and the eLogbook (procedures, urgency, supervision level). The article states "All databases used are mandatory repositories of surgical training data in the UK." Complete training records, reviewed regularly by supervisors, are described as adding reliability to the data.
requirements: Requires mandatory, centrally held data collection with unique-identifier linkage and defined supervision-code descriptors
constraints: Trainees lacking complete stage-of-training dates were excluded, and procedures recorded as observed or not counting toward certification were excluded from analysis
target_learning_goals: Tracking operative experience, supervision level, and competency assessment outcomes
examples: The study identified 360 completers, excluded 49 without complete stage dates, and analyzed 311 trainees' full records
key_sources: Elsey EJ, Griffiths G, West J, Humes DJ. (2018). Changing Autonomy in Operative Experience Through UK General Surgery Training: A National Cohort Study. Annals of Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1097/SLA.0000000000003032
